{
  "content":"# 312 — Same-language wire fast path: dual-ring slot, JSON at language borders\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nToday every wire's bytes are whatever the producing spec wrote, and\nthe consuming spec reads them verbatim. The Lua spec emits JSON via\n`lua_native_to_json` (`langs/lua/spec.c:335`); the C and Bash specs\nhave no bridge implementations yet and only carry whatever bytes\ntheir bytes-in-bytes-out `invoke` produced.\n\nThe dispatch layer picks the spec callback (`invoke_native` /\n`invoke_json` / fallback `invoke`) based on a single per-box\n`use_native_invoke` bit computed at graph load — true only when\n**every** input edge and **every** output edge of the box stays\nwithin one language. That's the pessimistic per-box approximation:\na box whose output fans to one same-language consumer and one\ncross-language consumer is classified as cross-language for the\nwhole box, so the same-language neighbor eats the JSON cost too.\n\nThe wire-format design question — what shape the slot has when\nsame-language hops should stay native and JSON should only show up\nat language borders — has not been settled in code. This issue\nsettles it.\n\n## Intended behavior — dual-ring slot\n\n**Each input slot is two ring buffers plus an ordering ring.**\n\n```\nslot {\n    ring_native  : ring of cells holding consumer-lang's native bytes\n    ring_json    : ring of cells holding JSON bytes (cross-language values)\n    ring_order   : ring of (which_ring, idx) tuples in arrival order\n    ... existing peek / pop modes apply to ring_order ...\n}\n```\n\n**Producer push** (per outgoing connection):\n\n- If the connection's per-edge bit `output_edge_native[j]` is true,\n  the producer's spec writes its native bytes to the consumer\n  slot's `ring_native`.\n- Otherwise the spec converts to JSON via `native_to_json` and\n  writes to `ring_json`.\n- Either way, push a `(which_ring, idx)` tuple to `ring_order`.\n\n**Consumer pop**:\n\n- Pop `ring_order` to learn which ring the next value lives in.\n- Pop the cell at the indicated index in the indicated ring.\n- The consumer's spec receives a `(native | json, bytes)` pair per\n  input and picks the matching decoder.\n\nThis shape is precise on **mixed fan-in ports**: a port fed by one\nLua producer and one C producer keeps the Lua values native in\n`ring_native` and the C-translated-to-JSON values in `ring_json`.\nThe consumer pays JSON-decode cost only on cross-language cells,\nnot on the entire port. The per-port-classification alternative\n(slot is all-JSON if any fan-in is cross-lang) is the simpler\nfallback — strictly correct, but forces native producers to eat\nJSON on mixed-fan-in ports. Dual-ring keeps each cell at the\nright cost.\n\n### Per-language native bytes\n\nEach spec picks its own native byte format. The only contract is\ninternal symmetry: the spec's own native-write and native-read have\nto round-trip its own runtime values.\n\n- **Lua** — bytes the spec can deserialize back to a Lua value\n  quickly. Candidates: msgpack, `lua_dump` for closures, a custom\n  binary form. `cjson.encode` is a valid starting point (a JSON\n  string the Lua spec parses with `cjson.decode`); refine later if\n  profiling shows the encode/decode is hot.\n- **C** — `memcpy` of the typed struct. The C spec's generated\n  wrapper (issue 307) knows the layout, so the ring cell holds the\n  struct's bytes verbatim.\n- **Bash** — strings. Bash has no other native form; its native\n  ring stores string bytes directly.\n\n### Why JSON for the cross-language ring\n\nJSON's structure is self-describing — six kinds (object, array,\nnumber, string, bool, null), each with an obvious mapping into\nevery language's runtime. Adding a new language K means K's spec\nimplements one pair of bridges: `native_to_json` and\n`json_to_native`. No spec ever needs code that knows another\nlanguage's types. The N-language matrix collapses to N spec-pair\nimplementations, not N² pair-wise paths.\n\nThe harder cases — closures, opaque language values, function\npointers — don't fit JSON's structure. JSON carries them via\nsentinel primitives:\n\n- `$ref` — pointer + length + type tag for bytes in the large-value\n  heap. In-process specs deref directly; cross-process boundaries\n  inline the bytes at the UDS marshaller.\n- `$function_pointer` — in-process address + signature for\n  callables. Wire compile fails if the consumer's language can't\n  reconstruct.\n- `$lang_opaque` — \"these bytes are language-X-internal.\" The\n  destination spec either knows what to do or wire compile fails.\n\nFirst-cut behavior: `encode_value` in the Lua spec hard-errors on\nfunction / userdata / thread (`langs/lua/spec.c:317`). Sentinels\nland in a later slice.\n\n## Per-edge classification at graph load\n\nThe graph loader's single-threaded phase walks every connection\nand computes per-box arrays:\n\n- `input_edge_native[i]` — one bit per input port. True iff every\n  producer feeding that port shares the consumer's language.\n- `output_edge_native[j]` — one bit per outgoing connection. True\n  iff the consumer on the other end shares this box's language.\n\nBoth arrays are already declared and populated — see\n`src/010-graph-loader.h:145` and `src/010-graph-loader.c:689-754`.\n\nUnder dual-ring, only `output_edge_native[j]` is consulted on the\npush path (it picks the ring at write time). The consumer-side bit\n`input_edge_native[i]` is now informational — the actual per-cell\nring tag lives in `ring_order` and is precise per cell.\n\nThe per-box `use_native_invoke` summary is **removed**. The\ndispatch reads `ring_order` per pop and consults the cell's tag\ndirectly.\n\n### Why per-edge, not per-box\n\nThe earlier per-box approximation collapsed on the first\ncross-language edge it found — a Lua box with one C neighbor went\nJSON across all its other edges. Per-edge keeps the cost local to\nthe actual cross-language boundary. The interior of any\nsame-language island skips JSON; only the boundary edges pay. The\nimplementation cost is identical: same number of bits per box,\nstored per-port / per-connection instead of per-box.\n\nDual-ring takes precision one step further: even on a single port\nwith mixed fan-in, each individual cell is in the right ring. The\nboundary tightens from \"edges that cross languages\" to \"cells\nthat crossed languages.\"\n\n## Runtime dispatch\n\n### Input-read\n\nFor each input port:\n```c\n(which_ring, idx) = ring_order_pop(slot->ring_order)\ncell_bytes        = ring_at(which_ring == NATIVE ? slot->ring_native\n                                                  : slot->ring_json,\n                            idx)\ninput_data[i]   = cell_bytes\ninput_native[i] = (which_ring == NATIVE)\n```\n\n`input_native[i]` is a per-input flag the spec consults to know\nwhether `input_data[i]` is its native form or JSON.\n\n### Spec invoke\n\nThe spec's `invoke` signature gains per-input and per-output flags:\n\n```c\nint invoke(handle, file_path, fn_name,\n           const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes,\n           const int *input_native, int n_inputs,\n           int output_native,\n           void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity, int *out_size);\n```\n\nThe spec dispatches per input: if `input_native[i]`, decode as\nnative; else decode as JSON. The output is written in whatever\nform `output_native` indicates — one form, one write. The previously\nseparate `invoke_native` and `invoke_json` callbacks collapse into\nthis single dispatching `invoke`; the per-input dispatch is what\nthe design actually needs.\n\nFor boxes whose output fans to multiple consumers in different\nlanguages, the dispatch picks one form for `output_native` based\non whichever ring is dominant (typically native if any\nsame-language consumer exists; the cross-language consumers eat a\n`native_to_json` conversion at push time). The detail is a runtime\noptimization, not a correctness concern.\n\n### Output-push\n\n```c\nfor each outgoing connection j:\n    if output_edge_native[j]:\n        push native_bytes      to consumer->ring_native\n        push (NATIVE, idx)     to consumer->ring_order\n    else:\n        if output_was_native: json_bytes = spec->native_to_json(native_bytes)\n        push json_bytes        to consumer->ring_json\n        push (JSON, idx)       to consumer->ring_order\n```\n\nIf the spec produced native and multiple cross-language consumers\nexist, the dispatch calls `native_to_json` once and reuses the\nJSON bytes across every cross-language push (optimization, not\nrequired for correctness).\n\n## Edge cases\n\n- **All-same-language graph**: every connection's\n  `output_edge_native[j]` is true; `ring_json` stays unallocated\n  across every slot; activity is on `ring_native` and `ring_order`\n  only.\n- **All-different-language graph**: every connection routes to\n  `ring_json`; `ring_native` stays unallocated.\n- **Mixed fan-in**: both rings active on the same slot. Consumer\n  sees a mix of native and JSON cells, picked apart by\n  `ring_order`.\n- **Type changes mid-development**: a wire that was Lua→Lua\n  becomes Lua→C when the user changes a downstream box's language.\n  The graph loader recomputes the per-edge bits on the next load;\n  no data conversion at runtime, no migration.\n\n## Implementation cost\n\n- **Slot store**: two rings per slot instead of one, plus the\n  ordering ring. Allocate `ring_json` and `ring_order` lazily —\n  same-language-only slots pay nothing for them. Per-cell cost:\n  one extra ordering-ring write on push, one extra read on pop.\n- **Spec interface**: one signature change to the `invoke`\n  callback adding `input_native[]` and `output_native`. Every\n  spec's `invoke` gains a per-input branch. Lua's branch is\n  almost free — both decoders (`json_to_native` and the future\n  native one) already exist as bridges. C and Bash need their\n  JSON bridges written, which is shared with the broader\n  cross-language work in 307/308.\n- **Dispatch**: one extra step on read (consult ordering ring),\n  one extra branch on push (which ring to write).\n\nThe win is exactness: same-language values stay native even when\ntheir port has a cross-language sibling producer.\n\n## Future: whole-program same-language compilation (issue 313)\n\n313 describes merging all same-language source into one\ntranslation unit per language at compile time. The merge does\n**not** eliminate the slot store for same-language wires — boxes\nstill run as separate tasks in the thread pool, possibly on\ndifferent workers, so values still need a place to wait for\nsibling inputs to arrive. The thread pool's parallelism depends\non tasks being scheduled independently; collapsing same-language\nhops to direct function calls would serialize execution and defeat\nthe pool.\n\nWhat 313 thins is the **spec invocation overhead**: for boxes in\nthe merged region, the dispatch can call the function directly on\nthe worker's `lua_State` (or compiled C code) without going\nthrough dlsym + bytes-marshal + bridge. The dual-ring slot shape\nremains; 313 makes the native-ring's read/write cheaper. The two\nlayers stack, they don't cancel.\n\n## Resolved design choice: JSON, not type-annotated raw bytes\n\nAn earlier note asked whether cross-language wires should use\ntype-annotated raw byte encodings (length-prefixed ints, raw\nfloats, etc.) instead of JSON. **Decided: JSON across the board\nfor the cross-language ring.** Rationale:\n\n- JSON's self-describing structure makes a new language one\n  spec-pair of `native_to_json` / `json_to_native` — no per-pair\n  language paths.\n- The native ring's format is each spec's private choice, so the\n  per-language performance flexibility is there without universal\n  type-tag complexity.\n- Sentinel primitives in JSON (`$ref`, `$function_pointer`,\n  `$lang_opaque`) carry the structurally awkward cases without\n  forcing the wire format to grow new top-level shapes.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Extend the slot data structure**. Add `ring_native`,\n   `ring_json`, `ring_order` to the slot type in\n   `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}`. Allocate `ring_json` and\n   `ring_order` lazily.\n2. **Extend the spec `invoke` signature**. Update `lang_invoke_fn`\n   in `langs/lang-spec.h` to add `const int *input_native`,\n   `int output_native`. Touch every spec's `invoke` stub to accept\n   (and initially ignore) the new parameters.\n3. **Update dispatch input-read** (`src/012-dispatch.c`). Pop\n   `ring_order` first, then the named ring. Populate\n   `input_native[]` per input port.\n4. **Update dispatch output-push** (`src/012-dispatch.c`). Select\n   the consumer's ring based on `output_edge_native[j]`. Write\n   the ordering-ring tuple. Reuse JSON across cross-language\n   consumers when the producer fanned to multiple.\n5. **Lua spec** (`langs/lua/spec.c`). Branch per `input_native[i]`\n   — decode native or JSON accordingly. Pick the native byte\n   format (start with `cjson.encode`; refine later).\n6. **C and Bash spec bridges**. Implement `native_to_json` and\n   `json_to_native` for C and Bash so cross-language pushes work.\n   C's native form is `memcpy` of the wrapper's declared struct;\n   Bash's native form is plain strings.\n7. **Remove `use_native_invoke`**. Drop the per-box field from\n   `box_t` and its computation from `graph_load`. The dispatch\n   consults the ordering ring's per-cell tag, not a per-box\n   summary.\n8. **Tests**. A 100k-iteration Lua→Lua pipeline uses `ring_native`\n   exclusively. A mixed-lang pipeline exercises both rings. A\n   mixed-fan-in port shows both rings active on one slot.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}` — slot data structure; the\n  dual-ring extension lands here.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — per-edge classification (already\n  done at `010-graph-loader.c:689-754`).\n- `src/012-dispatch.{c,h}` — input-read, output-push.\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — `invoke` signature extension.\n- `langs/lua/spec.c`, `langs/c/spec.c`, `langs/bash/spec.c` — per-spec\n  implementations.\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — original single-ring\n  slot design (completed); the dual-ring extension is the structural\n  amendment captured here.\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md`, `307-c-language-spec.md`,\n  `308-bash-language-spec.md` — per-spec typed marshalling lands on\n  top of this issue.\n- `issues/313-research-whole-program-same-language-merge.md` —\n  follow-on that thins spec invocation for merged regions.\n- `issues/245-wire-color-by-cross-language-classification.md` —\n  editor-side visual reflection of the per-edge classification\n  (green for JSON, gray for native).\n\n## Implementation status\n\nWhat's in place:\n\n- `lang_spec_t` carries `invoke_native`, `invoke_json`,\n  `native_to_json`, `json_to_native` slots (current shape — to be\n  collapsed to a single `invoke` with per-input/per-output flags\n  per this issue).\n- Lua's `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` are real\n  (`langs/lua/spec.c:335` and `:437`).\n- `input_edge_native[]` and `output_edge_native[]` are computed at\n  graph load (`src/010-graph-loader.c:689-754`).\n- Per-box `use_native_invoke` summary is computed and consulted by\n  dispatch — to be removed.\n- Single-ring slot store (`src/009-slot-store.c`).\n\nWhat's still ahead:\n\n- Dual-ring slot shape (this issue's core).\n- Spec `invoke` signature extension (`input_native[]`,\n  `output_native`).\n- Dispatch reads from the ordering ring; push selects ring based\n  on `output_edge_native[j]`.\n- C and Bash bridges, plus native byte formats per language.\n- Removal of `use_native_invoke`.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Lua's native byte format**: start with `cjson.encode` (still a\n  win over the json-ring path because the consumer's spec\n  recognises its own format and skips a parse), or jump straight\n  to msgpack? Defer the decision; the dual-ring shape doesn't\n  depend on the choice.\n- **Sharing JSON across multiple cross-language consumers**: the\n  dispatch can call `native_to_json` once and push the same bytes\n  to N cross-language consumer slots. Worthwhile when N > 1; the\n  push path needs a small buffer to hold the JSON across the fan\n  loop. Implement after the basic path works.\n- **Bash native = JSON?**: Bash has no native form distinct from\n  strings, and JSON is already a string. Bash's native ring may\n  hold JSON-shaped strings (effectively aliasing the JSON ring's\n  content). Resolve by inspection once the bash spec writeup\n  starts.\n",

Done with the issue file edits. To your concern about agnostic JSON parsing:

**The "agnostic" part is JSON itself.** Six kinds — object, array, number, string, bool, null. Every language has an obvious mapping (Lua: object → table with string keys, array → table with `n` field for fidelity, number → Lua number, etc.). The Lua spec's `decode_node` at `langs/lua/spec.c:370` already does this in 60-ish lines. No type annotations on the wire are required because JSON's structure is self-describing — the parser sees `{` and knows it's an object; sees `42` and knows it's a number.

**Type annotations live in box JSON, not on the wire.** The consumer box's `inputs` array declares `{"name": "weight", "type": "int"}`. The spec uses that declaration to coerce or validate after parsing — if the JSON tree at that input slot is a string `"42"` but the box declared `int`, the spec parses-as-int or errors. The spec never has to ask "what type is this JSON value" — JSON tells it directly — and never has to know about *other* languages' types, just JSON and its own.

**Lua not having static annotations is fine.** Lua values are runtime-typed: every value carries its type tag (`LUA_TNUMBER`, `LUA_TSTRING`, etc.). The Lua spec inspects the value's type via `lua_type()` and writes the matching JSON kind. Symmetric on the way in. The spec's encoder at `langs/lua/spec.c:188` is the existing implementation.

**The genuinely hard cases — closures, file handles, opaque values — don't fit JSON's structure period.** Those get sentinel primitives (`$function_pointer`, `$lang_opaque`) inside the JSON, and any cross-language consumer that can't reconstruct fails at wire compile. There's no honest way to pass a Lua closure to a Bash box, so the wire is wrong, not the format.

So adding a new language K is genuinely just: K's spec implements `native_to_json` (walk K's values, emit JSON) and `json_to_native` (walk JSON, build K's values). N spec-pairs, never N². That's the whole reason JSON gets to be the universal ring format.

---

Recap of what I touched:

- **`issues/245-wire-color-by-cross-language-classification.md`** (new) — editor work, forest-green for cross-lang wires, gray for native, computed in `assets/js/006-wires.js`.
- **`issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md`** — rewrote to capture the dual-ring design (native ring + JSON ring + ordering ring per slot), per-edge push routing, the spec invoke signature change (collapsing `invoke_native` / `invoke_json` into one `invoke` with per-input/per-output flags), the resolved "JSON not type-annotated" question, and the corrected understanding of 313 (slot machinery stays; only spec invocation thins).
- **`docs/001-architecture.md`** — replaced the per-box `output_format` description with the dual-ring per-edge model.
- **Memory** — rewrote `project_cross_language_wire.md` to match.

306 and 307 didn't need rewriting — 312 now explicitly names them in its implementation sequence steps 5 and 6 (per-spec typed input dispatch + bridge implementations), so the dependency is captured.

Ready to start coding on slice 1 — extending the slot data structure with the dual-ring shape — whenever you are. Or did you want to look the issue rewrites over first?

the idea is, they'd use the well-defined spec for most things, and make a custom translation spec (which initializes to the default spec btw, to make it easier to apply edits or insert extra translation steps) for each of the weird options. Like if we need to turn a function pointer into a class method, but the C++ spec doesn't necessarily know that because it's just been presented with, like, a pointer to a spot in memory, and it's like... okay, what is that? who can say. But the user can say, and if we force them to make these little translation specs (also when we delete a box we should say "this box has a custom translation spec, are you sure you want to delete? the spec will be safe on disk if you want to re-use it later.") if we force them to make these, then they'll be A. more empowered to do things that are impossible to do agnostically, and B. we can relinquish the final responsibility of managing this part of the dataflow to the user. We'll do our best, and the language spec authors will try very hard, but some things might just be impossible without the user adding their own bit of glue code. Mostly because of the ambiguity between different language constructs. That stuff can't be known at runtime, or even at compile time. Only at "development time" is it possible.

There's no
   honest way to pass a Lua closure to a Bash box, so the wire is wrong, not the format.

That's a sharp escape hatch — pushing the genuinely-ambiguous cases back to the user, where the knowledge actually lives. Let me draft it as an issue. A couple of design points I want to lock down in the draft, raise them now so you can correct:

1. **What language is the custom spec written in?** Consumer's language, I'm assuming — so a C box's custom translation is C code, a Lua box's is Lua. Compiles / loads through the same spec machinery as the box's main function. The alternative is "always C" (universal) which would force Lua users into a foreign language for their shim.

2. **Custom translation replaces the default `(json|native)_to_native` step, but the dual-ring routing still applies.** Producer still picks a ring per `output_edge_native[j]`; consumer's custom translation sees the raw bytes plus a `which_ring` tag. So same-language same-shape cases bypass the custom spec entirely (default native pass-through still works). The custom spec only kicks in for the cases the default can't handle.

3. **Input side only for the first cut, output side as a follow-on?** Your description was about translation at the start of the consumer's task. A symmetric case exists — a Lua box wanting to *output* a closure runs into the default spec's hard-error on functions. The producer-side custom translation would serialize the closure (via `lua_dump` or whatever). Both sides exist; the user fills in either or both. I'll mention output-side in the issue's open questions so it's captured but not in the first slice.

4. **Default content of a freshly-created shim**: a literal copy of what the default spec would do, so the user can edit individual steps in place, vs. an empty stub that errors until filled in. I'm leaning the former — easier to add small tweaks than to write the whole decode from scratch.

Box-delete (the whole\n  box) with any custom translations attached prompts: \"this box\n  has N custom translation specs; the files stay on disk for\n  re-use, but the box's references will go.\" Confirm or cancel.\n\nThe \"file stays on disk if you delete the box\" rule means custom\ntranslations are identifiable by path, not by box. The user can\nattach the same file to a different box's port later, or delete\nthe file explicitly through a file-browser pane.\n\n## Lifecycle (runtime)\n\nThe dispatch's input-read step gains a per-port branch:\n\n```\nfor each input port i:\n    (which_ring, idx) = ring_order_pop(slot)\n    raw_bytes         = ring_at(...)\n    if box->inputs[i].custom_translation:\n        translated[i] = custom_translation[i](raw_bytes, which_ring)\n        input_native[i] = NATIVE   # custom shim output is always native\n    else:\n        translated[i] = raw_bytes\n        input_native[i] = (which_ring == NATIVE)\n```\n\nWhen the port has a custom shim, the shim does the decode and the\nspec's `invoke` sees native bytes (with `input_native[i] = NATIVE`).\nWhen the port has no custom shim, the default decode runs inside\nthe spec's invoke as today.\n\nThree consequences fall out from running on the consumer's worker:\n\n- A custom shim that does something slow or surprising holds the\n  consumer's worker, not the producer's. The producer is free as\n  soon as it's done writing raw bytes to the ring.\n- Each consumer eats its own translation cost; mixed fan-in\n  consumers translate cell-by-cell as they pop.\n- The custom shim is in the same language as the box's main\n  function, so it has full access to that language's runtime\n  (Lua tables, C structs, etc.) without crossing another\n  language boundary first.\n\n## Where it sits relative to the dual-ring (issue 312)\n\nThe dual-ring routing still applies. The producer chooses a ring\nper `output_edge_native[j]` as today. The consumer's per-port\ncustom shim sees the raw bytes plus the `which_ring` tag — so it\ncan distinguish \"these bytes are my own language's native format\"\nfrom \"these bytes are JSON from a cross-language producer\" and act\naccordingly.\n\nIn the easy cases (same-language same-shape), no custom shim is\nneeded; the default native pass-through still works. The custom\nshim earns its keep on the cells where the default\n`json_to_native` would error or produce something useless — that's\nwhere the user-written code takes over.\n\n## File layout\n\n```\nmaps/<name>/\n    boxes/\n        <box_id>.json                ← per-input port may reference translations/\n    translations/\n        <box_id>__<port_name>.<lang_ext>     ← per-port shim\n    src/\n        <box_id>.<lang_ext>                  ← box's main function\n```\n\nThe box JSON's `inputs` array grows an optional per-port field:\n\n```json\n{\n    \"id\": \"consume_class\",\n    \"lang\": \"c\",\n    \"ref\": \"consume.c\",\n    \"fn\": \"consume\",\n    \"inputs\": [\n        { \"name\": \"instance\", \"type\": \"bytes\",\n          \"custom_translation\": \"translations/consume_class__instance.c\" },\n        { \"name\": \"weight\",   \"type\": \"int\" }\n    ],\n    \"...\": \"...\"\n}\n```\n\nIf a port omits `custom_translation`, the default-spec decode runs\nfor that port as today. The `translations/` directory may contain\nshims with no attached port (orphaned, kept on disk by the\ndelete-doesn't-delete-file rule).\n\n## Custom translation function signature\n\nPer-port shims take one input's raw bytes and the `which_ring`\nflag, return one translated value in the consumer's native form.\nWorking draft for C:\n\n```c\nint sm_translate(const void *input_raw, int input_size,\n                 int input_native,\n                 void *output_native, int output_capacity,\n                 int *output_size);\n```\n\nLua's shape is analogous but in Lua-native terms — the function\ntakes a Lua string (the raw bytes) and a boolean (the native\nflag), returns the translated Lua value.\n\nOne signature per port keeps each shim's surface area exactly\nmatched to the port's job. A shim that needs to consult other\nports has a problem this design doesn't try to solve (per-port\nisolation is the principled choice); the user can fall back to\nplain decode-then-validate inside the box's main function for\ncross-port logic.\n\n## Default content of a freshly-created shim\n\nThe \"New\" button writes a file containing a literal copy of what\nthe default spec would do for that port's declared type. For C,\nthat's the small generated wrapper that parses `input_raw` per\nthe port's declared type and writes the result. For Lua, it's a\nfew lines that decode via the existing JSON / native helpers\nbased on `input_native`.\n\nThe user can run the shim without edits and behaviour matches the\nno-shim default. Edits typically replace one branch (the\nspecific weird case) and leave the rest alone. The \"starts as\ndefault, edits in place\" shape matches the project's preference\nfor upgrade paths over from-scratch authoring.\n\n## Compile pipeline (issue 309)\n\nThe compile pipeline already walks every box's `ref` to copy\nsource into `compiled/src/`. The same walk inspects each input\nport's `custom_translation` field and copies referenced files\ninto `compiled/translations/`. For C, each translation file\ncompiles to a `.so` alongside the box's main function. For Lua,\nfiles load into the worker's `lua_State` like any other Lua\nsource.\n\nWhen issue 313 (same-language source merge) lands, translation\nfiles get concatenated into the per-language bundle the same way\nbox main functions do — a translation file is just another\nfunction in the merged module.\n\n## Why this is the right escape hatch\n\nThe default spec contract is \"JSON is the universal interop, each\nspec handles its own native form, sentinels carry the in-process\nexotic cases on the producer side.\" That's enough for the\noverwhelming majority of data flow. The cases where it fails are\nexactly the cases where the user has knowledge the system can't\never infer — what a `void *` points to, how a serialized object\nis structured, which port is a discriminator for which other port.\n\nPushing those back to the user via a per-port shim is honest\nabout where the knowledge has to come from. It also lets the\ndefault spec contract stay narrow and predictable — the spec\nauthors don't have to chase every possible ambiguous receive-side\ntype with new special cases.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box state; per-input\n  `custom_translation` field read/write.\n- `assets/index.html` — inspector UI (New / View / Delete buttons\n  on each input-port row).\n- `src/006-server-main.lua` — HTTP backend for translation file\n  CRUD (path validation against `maps/<name>/translations/`).\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — load each input port's\n  `custom_translation` onto `box_t->inputs[i]`.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — input-read branch on\n  `box->inputs[i].custom_translation`.\n- `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` — package translation files into\n  the compiled map (issue 309).\n- `issues/245-wire-color-by-cross-language-classification.md` —\n  goldenrod-cheddar wires for ports with custom translations.\n- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — dual-ring shape\n  the translation slots into.\n- `issues/313-research-whole-program-same-language-merge.md` —\n  custom translations get merged alongside box source.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Box JSON schema**: add the optional per-input\n   `custom_translation` field. Graph loader reads it; absence\n   means default path for that port.\n2. **HTTP backend**: CRUD routes for translation files. Path\n   validation against `maps/<name>/translations/`.\n3. **Editor inspector**: New / View / Delete affordances on each\n   input-port row. \"New\" generates the file with\n   default-spec-equivalent contents parameterized on the port's\n   declared type. Easy\n  add to the existing compile validation; do once translations\n  exist as a feature.\n- **Shim author seeing cross-port context.** Per-port isolation\n  means a shim only sees its own input. A union whose\n  discriminator is in another port has to validate inside the\n  box's main function rather than in the shim. If a real\n  cross-port case shows up, the workaround is a follow-on\n  ticket — not a reason to abandon per-port isolation.\n",

No dedicated sentinel issue exists — they're mentioned descriptively in 312, 246, and the architecture doc, but the mechanics haven't been written down anywhere as a real design. They probably should be. Let me answer your questions first, then propose what to capture.

**Sentinel mechanics, walked through your function-pointer example.**

C box produces `int compare(void *, void *)`. The box JSON declares the output type as a function pointer with that signature. The C spec's `native_to_json` recognizes "this isn't a JSON-shaped value, it's a callable" and emits:

```json
{"$function_pointer": {"addr": "0x7fffabcd1234",
                       "signature": "int(void*,void*)"}}
```

The Lua consumer pops the JSON. Its `json_to_native` sees the `$function_pointer` sentinel and reconstructs the callable using **LuaJIT FFI** — code the Lua spec author wrote once:

```c
// Pseudocode inside lua_json_to_native when it sees $function_pointer
lua_getglobal(L, "ffi");
lua_getfield(L, -1, "cast");
lua_pushstring(L, signature);   // "int (*)(void*, void*)"
lua_pushinteger(L, addr);
lua_call(L, 2, 1);
// Stack top now holds an FFI callable Lua can call like a Lua function
```

The Lua box's user code then calls it normally — `compare_fn(a, b)` — and LuaJIT FFI does the actual C call. **In-process only**, because the address is a raw memory pointer that's only meaningful in this process.

No auto-generation in the general case. The spec author writes the reconstruction once per sentinel kind per language. For Python (hypothetical): `ctypes.CFUNCTYPE(...)`. For Bash: no FFI capability, so a wire carrying a function pointer to a Bash box **fails at compile time**. That's the "compile error if a cross-language wire ever points at a language that can't reconstruct" half of the design.

**`$ref` for large datasets** works the same shape, simpler:

```json
{"$ref": {"ptr": "0x...", "len": 1048576, "type": "bytes"}}
```

The bytes live in the large-value heap (`src/015-large-value-heap.c`). Refcount = number of consumer slots. Lua reads with `lua_pushlstring(ptr, len)` (copies into Lua's heap). C uses the pointer directly. Bash via UDS — the marshaller inlines the bytes at the socket boundary, since cross-process can't share a raw pointer. The user never knows it's a reference unless they care; it just looks like a value.

**`$lang_opaque`** — a tagged blob the producer's language wraps around a value it can't structurally describe (a Lua coroutine, a Python generator). The consumer either knows what to do (same language family) or wire compile fails. This is the catch-all when `$ref` and `$function_pointer` don't fit.

**The flexibility-vs-performance question — honest answer:**

It's not "huge flexibility cost recovered by threading." Threading is orthogonal parallelism, not a per-cell-cost reduction. The cost story is **paid per edge, where it actually occurs:**

- Same-language native wires: bytes pass through, no translation. Native ring of the slot.
- Cross-language wires: JSON encode + decode at the boundary. JSON ring of the slot. Bounded by value size.
- Sentinels: tiny — a few dozen bytes of JSON wrapping a pointer. The reconstruction is `ffi.cast` or equivalent: nanoseconds.
- Custom shims: whatever the user writes. Could be one line or could be a parser.

The "flexibility" doesn't impose a uniform tax. Primitives and structured data flow at JSON-parse cost across borders; same-language stays native; in-process references flow at pointer-copy cost via sentinels. Threading adds throughput on top by running boxes concurrently — but it doesn't make a JSON parse faster, it just lets two of them happen at once on different cores.

The real long-term optimization isn't threading-recovers-cost; it's **313's same-language merge** thinning the spec-invocation overhead inside same-language regions (no dlsym + marshal + bridge per call; the merged module is one big function pile and calls are direct). That's where the structural perf win lands, and it stacks cleanly on top of the dual-ring design.

---

Probably 318 since it's phase-3 runtime work that spec authors implement, not editor work.

Done with 246 broadening and 247 draft. Now your questions.

**Bash-via-compiled-binary as a `$function_pointer` alternative:** yes possible, and it's a real escape hatch worth knowing about — basically the CGI pattern, where the "function pointer" presented to Bash is a path to an executable Bash can spawn. The C spec would notice at compile time that a function-pointer output is wired to a cross-process consumer and emit a standalone binary instead of (or in addition to) the in-process address. Bash invokes it with `$(/path/to/binary arg1 arg2)` per call.

The cost: process spawn per call, 1–10 ms — exactly the phase-2 problem the spec system was built to eliminate. It's worth doing as an opt-in for the cases where you genuinely need C-from-Bash and you accept the cost. The mechanism slots into the broader sentinel-primitives design (issue I'm still pitching at 318): in the matrix of "consumer language can reconstruct `$function_pointer` →," Bash's cell goes from "compile error" to "spawn-via-binary, with the cost noted in the editor." Memory-allocation-into-shared-region is the further escape hatch and yes, that direction is operating-system shape — leave it for when there's a real demand.

**How 312 and 313 relate.**

**312 is the wire format.** Dual-ring slots, per-edge classification, JSON-only-at-borders. Defines how *values* move between boxes. Active every box invocation, every wire, every cell.

**313 is the spec invocation thinner.** Defines how *the function gets called* once dispatch has the inputs ready and is about to invoke. Default (post-312): the dispatch calls `spec->invoke(handle, file_path, fn_name, input_data, ...)` which does dlsym + bridge + lua_pcall. 313 says: for boxes in the merged same-language region, skip all that — the function is already a callable in the merged module loaded on the worker's lua_State, so dispatch calls it directly.

The layering, made concrete in one box invocation under both 312 and 313:

```
1. Worker picks up the task.
2. Dispatch reads inputs from the box's slots.        ← 312 (dual-ring slot)
3. Dispatch decides which function to call.
   - Default: look up spec by box->spec_idx, call its invoke
   - 313 merged region: function is already a known callable
     in the merged module; direct call.
4. Function runs, returns a value.
5. Dispatch writes output to consumer slots.          ← 312 (per-edge ring routing)
```

Steps 2 and 5 are 312's territory and are unchanged by 313. Step 3 is where they differ. The slot machinery stays alive in the merged region because tasks are still scheduled across worker threads — a producer on worker 0 and a consumer on worker 1 still need the slot to hand off the value. 313 doesn't collapse parallelism; it just makes the per-call overhead near-zero for in-region calls.

**Order I'd propose for the parallel work:**

1. **246 broadening** ✓ (just landed — the framing now covers same-language user-intervention, not just cross-language ambiguity).
2. **247 debug-lens** ✓ (drafted, ready for review — can build independently in parallel with everything else).
3. **312 slice 1** — extend the slot data structure with `ring_native`, `ring_json`, `ring_order`. Touches `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}`. Pure data-structure work, no dispatch or spec changes yet.
4. **312 slice 2** — extend the `lang_invoke_fn` signature with `input_native[]` / `output_native`. Touches `langs/lang-spec.h` and every spec's stub.
5. **313 written design** — the issue says the deliverable is a design doc, not code. Pick a small all-Lua graph (`maps/hello`), work out what the merged Lua file looks like, how dispatch identifies "this is a merged-region call" and gets the function pointer, how iterator boundaries are handled inside the merge. This is design-thinking work that can happen between 312 slices.
6. **312 slice 3** — dispatch input-read consults `ring_order`; output-push routes per `output_edge_native[j]`.
7. **312 slice 4** — Lua spec branches per `input_native[i]`. C / Bash bridges land here too (or in 307/308 — overlapping work).
8. **313 prototype** — implement the merged-Lua-file path. Now that 312 is real, 313 has a stable foundation to bolt onto.

312 slices 1, 2, 3, 4 are the unblocking core. 313 design can happen in parallel any time; 313 prototype waits for 312 to be in. 247 is fully independent.

Want me to start on 312 slice 1 now? Or take a pass at 313's written design first while you look 246/247 over?

{
  "content":"# 318 — Sentinel primitives in the cross-language JSON wire\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Concept\n\nJSON's structure covers six kinds of value cleanly — object,\narray, number, string, bool, null — and the cross-language ring\nin the dual-ring slot (issue 312) carries JSON for any wire that\ncrosses a language boundary. The structural cases that don't fit\nthose six kinds — Lua closures, libcurl handles, C++ class\ninstances, file handles, function pointers, large byte buffers\nwhere serialization would be expensive — need somewhere to live\nin the JSON ring without forcing the wire format to grow new\ntop-level shapes.\n\n**Sentinel primitives** are JSON object shapes with reserved key\nnames that mean \"this isn't a structural value, it's a reference\nto something the consumer must reconstruct using language-specific\nmachinery.\"\n\nThree kinds, each solving a different structural gap:\n\n```json\n{\"$ref\":              {\"ptr\": \"0x...\",  \"len\": 1048576,\n                       \"type\": \"bytes\"}}\n{\"$function_pointer\": {\"addr\": \"0x...\", \"signature\": \"int(void*,void*)\"}}\n{\"$lang_opaque\":      {\"lang\": \"lua\",   \"tag\": 12345,\n                       \"shape\": \"coroutine\"}}\n```\n\nSentinels are **emitted by the producer's spec** when its language\nhas a value JSON can't represent structurally. They are\n**reconstructed by the consumer's spec** using whatever runtime\nmachinery that language provides (LuaJIT FFI, ctypes for Python,\ndirect cast for C, etc.). Wires whose consumer cannot reconstruct\na sentinel kind **fail at compile time** — the editor catches the\nmismatch when the user wires a function-pointer output into a\nBash input.\n\n## Why these three, not more\n\nThe three sentinels carve up the structural gap by ownership:\n\n- **`$ref`** — bytes in a shared heap. The producer wrote the\n  bytes to the large-value heap (issue 302 / `src/015-large-value-heap.c`)\n  and emits a pointer-and-length reference. The bytes are\n  immutable for the wire's lifetime; refcount tracks consumers.\n  Solves: \"I have a megabyte to share; copying it through the\n  slot would be wasteful.\"\n- **`$function_pointer`** — a callable, identified by a raw\n  address and a signature interpretable in C-function-pointer\n  syntax. The address is process-local. The signature is the\n  contract between producer and consumer. Solves: \"I have a\n  function I want my consumer to be able to call directly.\"\n- **`$lang_opaque`** — a language-private value. The producer\n  tags it with the language name and a worker-private reference\n  the producer's spec can resolve back. Solves: \"I have a value\n  with no general structural representation; only my own\n  language knows what it is.\"\n\nAnything that doesn't fit one of the three either (a) has a\nJSON-structural representation and shouldn't be a sentinel, or\n(b) is genuinely unrepresentable and the wire is wrong, not the\nformat.\n\n## Producer protocol\n\nEach language spec's `native_to_json` walks its native values and\nemits the appropriate sentinel when it encounters a non-structural\nvalue. The spec author writes the emit logic; it's not generic.\n\n### Lua\n\n`encode_value` in `langs/lua/spec.c:188` currently hard-errors on\nfunction / userdata / thread / lightuserdata. The extension:\n\n- **Function** (`LUA_TFUNCTION`) — if the function is a C function\n  registered with FFI, emit `$function_pointer` with its FFI\n  signature; if it's a Lua function, emit `$lang_opaque` with\n  `lang: \"lua\"` and a tag the spec can use to resolve the\n  function back later (a registry index, for example).\n- **Userdata** with an FFI ctype — emit `$function_pointer` if\n  the type is a function pointer; `$ref` if the type is a sized\n  buffer; `$lang_opaque` otherwise.\n- **Coroutine** (`LUA_TTHREAD`) — `$lang_opaque` with\n  `shape: \"coroutine\"`.\n- **Large strings or tables** — at the spec's discretion, the\n  producer may write the value to the large-value heap and emit\n  `$ref` instead of inlining the bytes. Decision is per-call,\n  driven by size threshold or output annotation.\n\n### C\n\nThe C spec's generated wrapper (issue 307) knows the box's\ndeclared output type. The wrapper emits the right sentinel\nshape based on the type:\n\n- A declared `function_pointer` return — `$function_pointer`\n  with the type's signature.\n- A declared `bytes` return whose size exceeds the inline\n  threshold — `$ref` with the bytes written to the heap.\n- A declared opaque struct — `$lang_opaque` if the struct's\n  shape is C-only.\n\n### Bash\n\nBash has no native values besides strings; sentinels don't apply\non the emit side. A Bash producer always emits structural JSON\nstrings.\n\n## Consumer protocol\n\nEach spec's `json_to_native` walks the JSON tree and, when it\nsees a sentinel key, reconstructs the value using its language's\nmachinery. The reconstruction is the spec author's responsibility.\n\n### Lua\n\n```c\n// inside lua_json_to_native, on seeing {\"$function_pointer\": {...}}:\nconst char *sig = json_string_value(obj, \"signature\");\nuintptr_t   addr = json_int_value(obj, \"addr\");\nlua_getglobal(L, \"ffi\");\nlua_getfield(L, -1, \"cast\");\nlua_pushstring(L, sig);                 // \"int (*)(void*, void*)\"\nlua_pushinteger(L, (lua_Integer)addr);\nlua_call(L, 2, 1);\n// stack top: an FFI callable Lua can invoke as compare_fn(a, b)\n```\n\n`$ref` reconstruction in Lua copies the bytes (`lua_pushlstring(ptr, len)`)\nsince Lua's value model needs values in Lua's heap. The\nproducer's refcount handles the lifetime.\n\n`$lang_opaque` with `lang: \"lua\"` resolves the tag through the\nworker's per-worker registry; with `lang != \"lua\"` it's a wire\ncompile error.\n\n### C\n\nDirect casts. `$function_pointer` becomes a typed function\npointer the wrapper can invoke. `$ref` is a `(void*, size_t)`\npair the wrapper hands to the user's function. `$lang_opaque`\nwith `lang: \"c\"` is a typed-struct pointer; other langs fail.\n\n### Bash\n\nBash cannot reconstruct any sentinel except possibly `$ref`\n(by reading the bytes from the file the marshaller staged at the\nprocess boundary). `$function_pointer` and `$lang_opaque` fail\nunless the producer chose the cross-process escape hatch (see\nbelow).\n\n## Compile-time validation\n\nThe compile step walks every wire and checks:\n\n- If the producer's declared output type can emit sentinel kind\n  K (per the producer language's spec capability), then\n- The consumer's language must be able to reconstruct sentinel\n  kind K (per the consumer language's spec capability).\n- If not, **the compile fails** with the specific wire and the\n  specific sentinel kind named.\n\nThis is editor-time feedback. The user fixes the wire\n(reroute it, change the consumer's language, attach a custom\ntranslation per issue 246) before the program ever runs.\n\nThe per-spec capability is a static fact each spec declares.\nAdding a new language K declares K's emit set and reconstruct\nset; the compile validator consults the declaration.\n\n## Cross-process escape hatch for `$function_pointer`\n\nBash (and any other process-isolated language) can't dereference\nan in-process function-pointer address. Two options when a\nfunction pointer's wire targets such a consumer:\n\n1. **Fail at compile time** (the default). Clear, honest.\n2. **Producer-side compiled binary** (opt-in). When the C spec\n   detects that a function-pointer output is wired to a\n   cross-process consumer, it compiles the function into a\n   standalone executable in `compiled/cross-process/<box>__<port>.bin`.\n   The sentinel becomes:\n\n   ```json\n   {\"$function_pointer\": {\"binary\": \"compiled/cross-process/...\",\n                          \"signature\": \"int(int,int)\"}}\n   ```\n\n   Bash invokes the binary with `$(./bin args...)` per call. Cost:\n   process spawn per invocation (1-10 ms). The escape hatch is\n   opt-in per box output — the user explicitly chooses the cost\n   in the inspector.\n\nThe default behaviour is option 1 because hiding the spawn cost\nwould mislead the user about runtime behaviour. The user picks\ntheir language; the cost follows from the choice. Option 2 is\nthe escape hatch for cases where the user genuinely needs\nC-from-Bash and accepts the cost.\n\n## Relationship to custom translation specs (issue 246)\n\nSentinels are the **spec author's tool** for representing\nnon-structural values. Custom translations are the **user's\ntool** for interpreting them (or any other value) when the\ndefault reconstruction isn't what they want.\n\nThe escalation path:\n\n1. Default spec encode / decode handles JSON-structural values\n   transparently.\n2. When the producer's value can't be encoded structurally, the\n   spec author's emit logic produces the right sentinel.\n3. When the consumer's spec can reconstruct the sentinel\n   generically (FFI cast, ctypes, direct pointer), the default\n   reconstruction runs.\n4. When the user wants a different interpretation than the\n   default (treat a function pointer as a method on a class\n   instance, dereference a `$ref` and parse its bytes as a\n   custom format, etc.), they attach a per-port custom\n   translation that overrides the default reconstruction.\n\nSo sentinels and custom translations are layered: sentinels\nprovide the *bytes that arrive at the wire* for non-structural\nvalues; custom translations decide *what to do with those bytes*\nwhen the default isn't enough.\n\n## Where in the dispatch this lives\n\nSentinels live inside the JSON ring of the dual-ring slot. The\nslot store (issue 312) doesn't know about them — it just carries\nbytes. The producer's `native_to_json` emits them when writing\nto the JSON ring; the consumer's `json_to_native` recognizes\nand reconstructs them when reading from the JSON ring.\n\nInside the native ring, sentinels don't appear — native values\nare encoded in the language's own binary form, which can\nrepresent its own callables / opaque values directly without\nneeding a JSON-side hack.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — bridges (`native_to_json`,\n  `json_to_native`) are where sentinel handling lives per spec.\n- `langs/lua/spec.c:188` (`encode_value`) — emit-side extension\n  point. Currently hard-errors on function / userdata / thread;\n  this issue replaces those errors with sentinel emission.\n- `langs/lua/spec.c:370` (`decode_node`) — reconstruct-side\n  extension point. Add sentinel recognition before generic\n  object handling.\n- `langs/c/spec.c` — C spec's `native_to_json` / `json_to_native`\n  (currently NULL); both grow when this issue lands.\n- `langs/bash/spec.c` — Bash spec; only `$ref` is reconstructable.\n- `src/015-large-value-heap.c` — `$ref` storage.\n- `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` — compile-time wire validation\n  walks producer/consumer sentinel capabilities.\n- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — dual-ring shape;\n  sentinels ride inside its JSON ring.\n- `issues/246-custom-translation-specs-per-port.md` — user-side\n  override layered on top of sentinel reconstruction.\n- `docs/001-architecture.md` — wire format section; gains a brief\n  sentinel reference.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Define the canonical JSON shapes**. Three sentinel kinds,\n   exact key names, value-object schemas. Document in\n   `docs/001-architecture.md`.\n2. **Lua emit**: replace the hard-errors in `encode_value` with\n   sentinel emission per the producer protocol above. Start with\n   `$function_pointer` for FFI callables and `$lang_opaque` for\n   Lua functions / coroutines.\n3. **Lua reconstruct**: extend `decode_node` to recognize the\n   three sentinels and reconstruct them.\n4. **Per-spec capability declarations**. Each spec declares its\n   emit set (sentinel kinds it can produce) and reconstruct set\n   (sentinel kinds it can consume). Lives next to the\n   `lang_spec_t` declaration.\n5. **C spec sentinels**. Emit via the generated wrapper based on\n   declared output types; reconstruct via direct cast.\n6. **Bash spec sentinels**. Only `$ref` on the reconstruct side\n   (read bytes from the marshaller's staged file).\n7. **Compile-time validation**. Walk every wire; check the\n   producer's emit set against the consumer's reconstruct set;\n   fail with a clear message on mismatch.\n8. **Cross-process escape hatch for `$function_pointer`**.\n   Opt-in flag in the box output declaration; the C spec emits a\n   standalone binary instead of (or alongside) the in-process\n   address.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **`$ref` lifetime across iterator-fed slots**. A producer's\n  output is referenced by an N-cell ring of consumer slots; each\n  cell holds the `$ref`, each pop decrements. Already supported\n  by the large-value heap's refcount, but worth verifying the\n  test coverage when sentinels land.\n- **Sentinel inside sentinel.** A `$ref` whose bytes are\n  themselves JSON containing a `$function_pointer` is legal but\n  weird. Document the recursive case; probably falls out of the\n  walker for free.\n- **Versioning the sentinel format**. The reserved key names\n  (`$ref`, `$function_pointer`, `$lang_opaque`) and the\n  value-object schemas are part of the compile-time contract.\n  Changing them is breaking. Worth a one-line stability note\n  somewhere.\n- **Cross-process `$ref` semantics**. In-process `$ref` is a raw\n  pointer + length. Cross-process (Bash via UDS), the marshaller\n  stages the bytes at the socket boundary. Decide whether the\n  Bash-side `$ref` reconstruction reads from a file path or\n  inlines the bytes in the request. The latter is simpler; the\n  former scales to bigger values.\n",

26	For Bash: probably no benefit — Bash is already process-per-call;
27	fusing scripts doesn't help much. Skip.
28	
29	## Why this is research, not a feature
30	
31	Three open questions that need code-level investigation before
32	the design is concrete:
33	
34	1. **Loop and iterator boundaries**: a same-language region with an
35	   iterator inside it has dynamic re-spawning. Is the iterator
36	   merged in (a loop in the generated code) or does it remain a
37	   spec-mediated boundary? If the latter, the merge buys less.
38	2. **Compile time**: whole-program optimization is slow. Does the
39	   incremental-compile model (issue 309's mtime check) still apply,
40	   or do edits require a full rebuild of the merged region?
41	3. **Debug story**: a stack trace inside the merged region needs to
42	   point back to a specific box. Either source-map-style mapping or
43	   per-function preserved names — both have costs.
44	
45	The right way to answer these is to prototype: take a small all-Lua
46	graph (like the hello map) and see what a merged version looks
47	like, both for runtime cost and for build-system complexity. The
48	prototype should be able to fall back to the per-box path if the
49	merge fails for any reason.
50	
51	## Why blocked until rest of phase 3 completes
52	
53	The merge optimization piggybacks on the per-box model — same
54	specs, same compile callback, same dispatch layer for cross-language
55	wires. Building it before the per-box model is settled risks
56	designing against a target that's still moving. After phase 3 ships
57	and the per-box path is stable, the merge becomes a clean
58	"everything except spec invocation gets shorter for this region."
59

8	 *     then cell_capacity bytes of payload. Untagged slots use the
9	 *     standard head/tail ring discipline; tagged slots use head/tail

ts: 2026-05-21T22:51:36.172Z

Before I dive into the slot store code — quick API check, since this affects every spec and the dispatch layer downstream.

Proposed surface for slice 1:

**New constants in `009-slot-store.h`:**
```c
SLOT_FLAG_DUAL_RING   = 1 << 3
SLOT_RING_NATIVE      = 0
SLOT_RING_JSON        = 1
```

**Slot allocation:** existing `slot_alloc(s, cell_capacity, n_cells, flags)` accepts the new flag. When set, the slot internally manages three rings (native, json, order) under one lock. The native ring uses the existing fields (no layout churn for non-dual slots); json and order rings are additional fields that are NULL on non-dual slots.

**New push/pop API:**
```c
int     slot_push_native (s, id, data, size, tag);
int     slot_push_json   (s, id, data, size, tag);
int32_t slot_pop_ordered (s, id, buf, buf_size, int32_t *out_which_ring);
```

For dual-ring slots: `slot_push_native` writes to native ring + ordering tuple under one lock; `slot_push_json` mirrors; `slot_pop_ordered` reads ordering ring first, then the indicated data ring.

For non-dual slots (backward compat): `slot_push_native` aliases to existing `slot_push`. `slot_push_json` returns -1 (not a dual-ring slot). `slot_pop_ordered` aliases to `slot_pop` and sets `*out_which_ring = SLOT_RING_NATIVE`.

Existing `slot_push` / `slot_pop` continue to work on non-dual slots unchanged. On a dual-ring slot they return -1 (caller must use the dual-aware functions).

**Internal: one lock per slot covers all three rings.** Atomic data + ordering write. No multi-slot races for the dispatch layer to worry about.

**Tests** added for: alloc dual slot, mixed push order preserved on pop, error on calling single-ring API on dual slot, lazy json-ring allocation works.

Match what you had in mind, or do you want to change anything (naming, ring-ordering encoding, lazy vs. eager allocation)?

398	    int large = (r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE) != 0;
399	
400	    lock_slot(r);
401	
402	    uint32_t head = atomic_load_explicit(&r->head, memory_order_acquire);
403	    uint32_t tail = atomic_load_explicit(&r->tail, memory_order_acquire);
404	    if (head == tail) {
405	        unlock_slot(r);
406	        return -1;
407	    }
408	
409	    uint32_t i = head % r->n_cells;
410	    uint32_t fs = cell_filled(r, i);
411	    if (fs == 0) {
412	        unlock_slot(r);
413	        return -1;
414	    }
415	    if ((uint32_t)buf_size < fs) {
416	        unlock_slot(r);
417	        return -1;
418	    }
419	    if (fs > 0) {
420	        if (large) {
421	            ua_chunk_t *chunk = NULL;
422	            memcpy(&chunk, cell_data(r, i), sizeof(void *));
423	            if (chunk) memcpy(buf, ua_data(chunk), fs);
424	        } else {
425	            memcpy(buf, cell_data(r, i), fs);
426	        }
427	    }
428	    /* head not advanced — peek leaves the cell in place and the
429	     * chunk's reference count untouched. */
430	    unlock_slot(r);
431	    return (int32_t)fs;
432	}
433	/* }}} */
434	
435	/* {{{ Local helper — find_lowest_tag_index() */
436	/* Return the in-ring cell index with the lowest tag among filled
437	 * cells. The caller holds the slot lock. Returns UINT32_MAX if no
438	 * filled cells exist. */
439	static uint32_t find_lowest_tag_index(slot_rec_t *r)
440	{
441	    uint32_t best     = UINT32_MAX;
442	    uint32_t best_tag = UINT32_MAX;
443	    for (uint32_t i = 0; i < r->n_cells; i++) {
444	        if (cell_filled(r, i) == 0) continue;
445	        uint32_t t = cell_tag(r, i);
446	        if (best == UINT32_MAX || t < best_tag) {
447	            best     = i;
448	            best_tag = t;
449	        }
450	    }
451	    return best;
452	}
453	/* }}} */
454	
455	/* {{{ slot_pop() */
456	int32_t slot_pop(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id,
457	                 void *buf, int32_t buf_size)
458	{
459	    slot_rec_t *r = get_slot(s, id);
460	    if (!r)                                  return -1;
461	    if (r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER) return -1;
462	    if (buf_size < 0 || (!buf && buf_size > 0)) return -1;
463	
464	    lock_slot(r);
465	
466	    uint32_t pick;
467	    if (r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED) {
468	        pick = find_lowest_tag_index(r);
469	        if (pick == UINT32_MAX) { unlock_slot(r); return -1; }
470	    } else {
471	        uint32_t head = atomic_load_explicit(&r->head, memory_order_acquire);
472	        uint32_t tail = atomic_load_explicit(&r->tail, memory_order_acquire);
473	        if (head == tail) { unlock_slot(r); return -1; }
474	        pick = head % r->n_cells;
475	    }
476	
477	    uint32_t fs = cell_filled(r, pick);
478	    if (fs == 0)                  { unlock_slot(r); return -1; }
479	    if ((uint32_t)buf_size < fs)  { unlock_slot(r); return -1; }
480	
481	    /* For LARGE_VALUE we capture the chunk handle here so we can
482	     * release it AFTER the slot lock is dropped — the allocator
483	     * takes its own mutex during ua_unref, and nesting the two is
484	     * fine but unnecessary if we can release the cheap lock first. */
485	    ua_chunk_t *released_chunk = NULL;
486	
487	    if (fs > 0) {
488	        if (r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE) {
489	            memcpy(&released_chunk, cell_data(r, pick), sizeof(void *));
490	            if (released_chunk) memcpy(buf, ua_data(released_chunk), fs);
491	        } else {
492	            memcpy(buf, cell_data(r, pick), fs);
493	        }
494	    }
495	
496	    /* Mark cell empty. For LARGE_VALUE cells, also zero the handle
497	     * so a stale chunk pointer can't be misread by a later inspector
498	     * — the actual release happens after we drop the slot lock. */
499	    uint32_t zero = 0;
500	    memcpy(cell_ptr(r, pick), &zero, sizeof zero);
501	    if (r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE) {
502	        ua_chunk_t *null_chunk = NULL;
503	        memcpy(cell_data(r, pick), &null_chunk, sizeof(void *));
504	    }
505	
506	    /* For untagged: advance head by one. For tagged: walk head
507	     * forward over any contiguous empty cells (the head/tail
508	     * relationship is preserved so further pushes still land at the
509	     * right spot, but stale empties at the front of the ring don't
510	     * block future pushes that wrap). */
511	    if (!(r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED)) {
512	        uint32_t head = atomic_load_explicit(&r->head, memory_order_relaxed);
513	        atomic_store_explicit(&r->head, head + 1u, memory_order_release);
514	    } else {
515	        uint32_t head = atomic_load_explicit(&r->head, memory_order_relaxed);
516	        uint32_t tail = atomic_load_explicit(&r->tail, memory_order_relaxed);
517	        while (head < tail && cell_filled(r, head % r->n_cells) == 0) {
518	            head++;
519	        }
520	        atomic_store_explicit(&r->head, head, memory_order_release);
521	    }
522	
523	    unlock_slot(r);
524	
525	    /* Drop the consumer's reference to the chunk now that the slot
526	     * lock is gone. The bytes have already been copied into the
527	     * caller's buffer, so reclamation is safe. If the refcount goes
528	     * to zero, the chunk rejoins the allocator's free-lists with an
529	     * eager neighbor-merge — the line that turns the old leak into
530	     * proper reclamation. */
531	    if (released_chunk) ua_unref(s->heap, released_chunk);
532	
533	    return (int32_t)fs;
534	}
535	/* }}} */
536	
537	/* {{{ slot_read_inc() */
538	uint32_t slot_read_inc(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, uint32_t mod)
539	{
540	    slot_rec_t *r = get_slot(s, id);
541	    if (!r)                                     return UINT32_MAX;
542	    if (!(r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER)) return UINT32_MAX;
543	    if (mod == 0)                               return UINT32_MAX;
544	
545	    uint32_t prev = atomic_fetch_add_explicit(&r->counter, 1u,
546	                                              memory_order_relaxed);
547	    return prev % mod;
548	}
549	/* }}} */
550	
551	/* {{{ slot_has_value() */
552	int slot_has_value(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id)
553	{
554	    slot_rec_t *r = get_slot(s, id);
555	    if (!r) return 0;
556	    if (r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER) return 1;
557	
558	    if (r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED) {
559	        /* Tagged: any filled cell counts. Cheap scan; tagged slots
560	         * are usually small. */
561	        lock_slot(r);
562	        int found = 0;
563	        for (uint32_t i = 0; i < r->n_cells; i++) {
564	            if (cell_filled(r, i) != 0) { found = 1; break; }
565	        }
566	        unlock_slot(r);
567	        return found;
568	    }
569	
570	    uint32_t head = atomic_load_explicit(&r->head, memory_order_acquire);
571	    uint32_t tail = atomic_load_explicit(&r->tail, memory_order_acquire);
572	    return head != tail;
573	}
574	/* }}} */
575	
576	/* {{{ slot_store_allocator() */
577	struct ua *slot_store_allocator(slot_store_t *s)
578	{
579	    return s ? s->heap : NULL;
580	}
581	/* }}} */
582	
583	/* {{{ slot_store_large_value_bytes_in_use() */
584	/* A small accessor for the reclamation regression test in issue
585	 * 302. Exposes the unified allocator's in-use byte total without
586	 * leaking the allocator type into the slot store's public API. */
587	uint64_t slot_store_large_value_bytes_in_use(slot_store_t *s)
588	{
589	    if (!s || !s->heap) return 0;
590	    return ua_bytes_in_use(s->heap);
591	}
592	/* }}} */
593	
594	/* {{{ slot_fill_count() */
595	int32_t slot_fill_count(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id)
596	{
597	    slot_rec_t *r = get_slot(s, id);
598	    if (!r)                                  return 0;
599	    if (r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER) return 0;
600	
601	    if (r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED) {
602	        lock_slot(r);
603	        int32_t n = 0;
604	        for (uint32_t i = 0; i < r->n_cells; i++) {
605	            if (cell_filled(r, i) != 0) n++;
606	        }
607	        unlock_slot(r);
608	        return n;
609	    }
610	
611	    uint32_t head = atomic_load_explicit(&r->head, memory_order_acquire);
612	    uint32_t tail = atomic_load_explicit(&r->tail, memory_order_acquire);
613	    return (int32_t)(tail - head);
614	}

Empty ring → nothing to pop. */\n    uint32_t oh = atomic_load_explicit(&r->order_head, memory_order_acquire);\n    uint32_t ot = atomic_load_explicit(&r->order_tail, memory_order_acquire);\n    if (oh == ot) { unlock_slot(r); return -1; }\n\n    uint32_t oi = oh % r->n_cells;\n    uint8_t *op = r->order_cells + (size_t)oi * ORDER_CELL_RECORD;\n    uint32_t which_ring, idx;\n    memcpy(&which_ring, op,     sizeof which_ring);\n    memcpy(&idx,        op + 4, sizeof idx);\n\n    /* Pick the indicated data ring's head pointer and cell array. */\n    _Atomic uint32_t *data_head;\n    uint8_t          *data_cells;\n    if (which_ring == (uint32_t)SLOT_RING_NATIVE) {\n        data_head  = &r->head;\n        data_cells = r->cells;\n    } else {\n        data_head  = &r->json_head;\n        data_cells = r->json_cells;\n    }\n\n    uint8_t *dp = data_cells + (size_t)idx * r->cell_record;\n    uint32_t fs;\n    memcpy(&fs, dp, sizeof fs);\n    if (fs == 0)                  { unlock_slot(r); return -1; }\n    if ((uint32_t)buf_size < fs)  { unlock_slot(r); return -1; }\n\n    if (fs > 0) memcpy(buf, dp + 4, fs);\n\n    /* Mark the data cell empty. */\n    uint32_t zero = 0;\n    memcpy(dp, &zero, sizeof zero);\n\n    /* Advance both heads. The data ring's head matches the ordering\n     * entry's idx at this point (entries are popped strictly in push\n     * order, and each data ring fills sequentially), so head + 1 is\n     * always the next-to-pop cell on that ring. */\n    uint32_t dh = atomic_load_explicit(data_head, memory_order_relaxed);\n    atomic_store_explicit(data_head,      dh + 1u, memory_order_release);\n    atomic_store_explicit(&r->order_head, oh + 1u, memory_order_release);\n\n    unlock_slot(r);\n\n    if (out_which_ring) *out_which_ring = (int32_t)which_ring;\n    return (int32_t)fs;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ slot_read_inc() */"

2. **The slider is per-input-port, not per-box**, and lives on `read` (or any) boxes inside the sub-map. Three binding kinds — positional / numbered / named — captured in an `external` block on the port.
3. **Output ports come from the sub-map's `write` boxes**. They keep their disk-write side effect AND emit their `value` input upward as part of the packed output blob.
4. **Output packed format matches your description literally**: 4-byte little-endian sizes, NULL-terminated size array, then data sections packed end-to-end. Offset arithmetic exactly as you described.
5. **Compile-time inlining vs. runtime sub-graph dispatch** is left as an open question with both paths sketched. Compile-time inlining composes more cleanly with 313's same-language merge; runtime dispatch is more flexible for hot-reload. Prototype picks one.

196	When off, the port behaves normally (wires-in or literal-value).
197	
198	A map with no marked inputs encapsulates to a no-input box (just
199	a source of write-box outputs). A map with no write boxes
200	encapsulates to a box with no output (side-effecting only —

202	
203	### Visual on the canvas
204	
205	The encapsulating box renders distinctly — different border,
206	maybe a small "sub-map" badge — so the user sees at a glance
207	that this isn't a leaf call. Hovering shows the sub-map's name
208	and a small thumbnail of its graph.
209	
210	## Runtime model
211	
212	Two implementation paths exist; pick after prototyping.
213	
214	**A. Compile-time inlining.** At compile (issue 309), the
215	encapsulating box is replaced by its sub-graph: every internal
216	box gets a prefixed id (`<encap_id>__<internal_id>`), every
217	internal wire stays internal, marked-input boxes get their
218	external bindings hooked to the parent's incoming wires, and
219	write boxes get their outputs hooked into the packing-into-blob
220	machinery. The runtime never sees encapsulation — one flat
221	graph. Composes cleanly with issue 313's same-language merge.
222	
223	**B. Runtime sub-graph dispatch.** The graph loader builds the
224	sub-map as a child graph, and the encapsulating box's task
225	spawns a sub-run that drives the child graph to quiescence,
226	collects its write-box outputs, packs them, and emits. The
227	child runs on the same thread pool — its tasks are just normal
228	pool tasks distinguished by their box-id namespace.
229	
230	Compile-time inlining is the cleaner design for performance and
231	debugging (one flat task pool, no recursion in the dispatch
232	layer). Runtime sub-graph dispatch is the more flexible design
233	for hot-reload and dynamic linking (the parent doesn't need to
234	recompile when the sub-map changes). The prototype picks one;
235	the alternative remains an open question until profile data
236	justifies the choice.
237	
238	Recursion (a sub-map encapsulates another sub-map) falls out of
239	either path naturally — inlining recurses through; runtime
240	dispatch recurses through. Cycles between maps are a compile-time
241	error.
242

246	  entry point for the "encapsulate" action.
247	- **Issue 239 (literal port shrinks to nodule)** — the

{
  "content":"# 249 — Tap input mode: radial-bubble ports and emoji box labels\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Concept\n\nThe editor's wire-connection affordance assumes a mouse — small\nports on the side of each box that the user clicks and drags\nbetween. On a touch screen those ports are awkward: hard to hit\nprecisely, easy to misfire. The full box header eats vertical\nspace that's even more precious on phone-sized canvases.\n\n**Tap input mode** is a parallel interaction model that the user\ntoggles into for touch-first editing:\n\n1. **Wires are formed via a radial-bubble menu.** Tap a box and\n   a ring of larger bubbles fans out around it, one bubble per\n   input port plus one per output port. The bubbles are large\n   enough to hit comfortably with a fingertip. Drag a bubble to\n   another box's bubble to wire them together; tap a bubble to\n   open its inspector menu (same content as the desktop's\n   per-port inspector).\n2. **Box headers shrink to four emoji.** The box's filename +\n   function name (which is long and hard to scan on small\n   screens) is replaced by four emoji glyphs the user picks.\n   Four characters of visual identity. Tap the box itself (not\n   a bubble) to see the full name in a popover.\n\nThe mode is intended to live alongside the current\nmouse-and-port model, not replace it. A user with a desktop and\na mouse keeps the existing affordances; a user with a tablet or\nphone flips to tap mode. The data model (boxes, wires, port\ndeclarations) is unchanged — only the editor's rendering and\ninteraction code branches on the mode.\n\n## Tap-mode wire connection — the radial bubble menu\n\nWhen the user taps a box in tap mode:\n\n```\n              ┌───────┐\n              │ port  │\n              │ bubble│\n              └───────┘\n         ┌───────┐         ┌───────┐\n         │ port  │         │ port  │\n         │ bubble│         │ bubble│\n         └───────┘         └───────┘\n                ┌──────────────┐\n                │  🧮📊✨🔢   │  ← the box (4 emoji)\n                └──────────────┘\n         ┌───────┐         ┌───────┐\n         │ port  │         │ port  │\n         │ bubble│         │ bubble│\n         └───────┘         └───────┘\n              ┌───────┐\n              │ out   │\n              │ bubble│\n              └───────┘\n```\n\n- One bubble per input port, distributed around the top / left /\n  right of the box.\n- One bubble per output port (or output branch, for comparator /\n  iterator boxes), distributed around the bottom.\n- Each bubble is sized for a fingertip — roughly 48×48 px at the\n  default zoom, scaling with the canvas.\n- Bubbles are labeled with the port name, abbreviated if\n  necessary.\n\nTwo gestures on a bubble:\n\n- **Tap** — opens the per-port inspector menu (literal-value\n  field, optional toggle, type selector, etc.). Same content as\n  the desktop inspector's port row, just rendered as a sheet\n  panel that pops up from the bottom of the canvas.\n- **Drag** — initiates a wire connection. As the finger moves,\n  a wire-in-progress follows the touch point. Drag onto another\n  box's bubble (the target box's radial menu pops up\n  automatically once the drag enters its bounding circle) and\n  release on the destination port bubble to complete the wire.\n\nCancellation: tap outside any bubble or box to close the radial\nmenu; release a drag over empty canvas to cancel the wire.\n\n### Multiple boxes selected\n\nIf the user has multiple boxes selected and taps the radial-menu\ntoggle, each selected box shows its own radial bubbles\nsimultaneously. Useful for wiring up a freshly-created cluster\nwithout tap-cycling.\n\n### Discoverability\n\nA small \"tap mode\" icon in the editor toolbar toggles the\nbehavior. The icon's state is persisted per-map (some maps the\nuser edits on a tablet, others on a desktop — the mode follows\nthe device choice for that map).\n\n## Four-emoji box labels\n\nIn tap mode, the box header renders as four emoji glyphs\ninstead of the filename + function name. The four emojis are\nchosen by the user via the box's inspector — a 4-cell editable\nfield, each cell a tap-to-pick emoji selector.\n\n```\n┌──────────────┐\n│  🧮📊✨🔢   │\n└──────────────┘\n```\n\nVisual properties:\n\n- Four cells, each a single emoji glyph at large size.\n- Default ordering reads left-to-right (no semantic meaning to\n  position; the user picks four glyphs that read together).\n- Box footprint shrinks accordingly — emoji-mode boxes are\n  smaller on the canvas, fitting more boxes in view on small\n  screens.\n- Tap the box body (not a bubble) → popover shows the full\n  filename + function name and any other identifying metadata.\n- Hover/long-press → same popover (for tablet stylus users).\n\n### Round-trip with desktop mode\n\nA box has both a textual label and four emoji slots in its JSON.\nDesktop mode shows the textual label; tap mode shows the emoji.\nThe two render independently from one stored shape:\n\n```json\n{\n    \"id\": \"compute_avg\",\n    \"label\": \"compute_avg\",      // textual, shown in desktop mode\n    \"emoji\": [\"🧮\", \"📊\", \"✨\", \"🔢\"],   // shown in tap mode\n    \"...\": \"...\"\n}\n```\n\nA box with no emoji set in tap mode falls back to a default\nglyph (the first letter of the function name framed in a\ncircle, say) so existing maps don't break when opened in tap\nmode.\n\n## Optional: auto-generated emoji labels via word embedding\n\nA more ambitious enhancement: when the user creates a new box\nor hasn't picked their emoji yet, the editor **suggests four\nemoji** by matching the box's textual identity against a pre-\ncomputed embedding space.\n\nSketch:\n\n1. Compute a text embedding of the box's `<filename>__<fn>`\n   string (e.g., `compute_avg__main`).\n2. Compute embeddings of every emoji in a curated list (the\n   emoji's keyword tags + common descriptions concatenated).\n   Embeddings are precomputed at editor build time and shipped\n   as a static lookup table.\n3. For each emoji, compute cosine similarity between the box's\n   embedding and the emoji's embedding.\n4. Pick the top four most-similar emojis.\n5. Present them in the box's emoji slots, with each slot\n   independently swap-able by the user.\n\nThis is a sometimes-works heuristic. A box named `parse_json`\nprobably gets 🗂️📄🔎🧩 or similar; a box named `compute_avg`\ngets something like 🧮📊∑✨. The user corrects when the\nheuristic misses — same affordance as the manual emoji picker.\n\nThe embedding model and the static lookup table are an editor-\nside dependency. Candidate models: a small local model\n(MiniLM, all-MiniLM-L6) bundled with the editor; or an\nembedding lookup precomputed offline and shipped as a JSON.\nThe precomputed-lookup option is heavier on disk but adds no\nruntime model dependency — likely the right tradeoff for an\neditor whose value proposition is \"runs as a Lua HTTP server\n+ static HTML.\"\n\nThis part is explicitly an enhancement, not part of the first\nslice. Persist via the\n   existing HTTP backend.\n2. **Tap-mode toggle**: toolbar button + per-map mode state.\n   In tap mode, the desktop port-and-wire affordances are\n   suppressed.\n3. **Emoji rendering**: in tap mode, box header renders the\n   `emoji` array (or a default if absent). Tap-the-body popover\n   shows the full label.\n4. **Emoji picker**: inspector for the box has four cells, each\n   a tap-to-pick emoji selector.\n5. **Radial bubble rendering**: on tap, fan out a circle of\n   port bubbles around the selected box.\n6. **Bubble tap → inspector sheet**: rendering and content for\n   the bottom-sheet port inspector.\n7. **Bubble drag → wire**: touch-drag handler; target-box\n   bubble-popup-on-hover; release-to-connect.\n8. **Multi-box selection radial behavior**: optional; defer if\n   straightforward composition doesn't fall out.\n9. **(Enhancement)** Auto-suggest emoji via embedding lookup:\n   ship a precomputed emoji-embedding table; pick top-4 on box\n   creation if user hasn't set the emoji field.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Emoji rendering on the canvas**: Canvas2D vs. DOM. 263	/* Caller frees the returned string. */
264	static char *resolve_path(const dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, const char *p)
265	{
266	    if (!p) return NULL;
267	    if (p[0] == '/') return strdup(p);             /* already absolute */
268	    const char *base = graph_map_dir(ctx->graph);
269	    if (!base) return strdup(p);
270	    size_t blen = strlen(base);
271	    size_t plen = strlen(p);
272	    char *out = malloc(blen + 1 + plen + 1);
273	    if (!out) return NULL;
274	    memcpy(out, base, blen);
